items.stem: Which of the following best describes "narrow AI"?
options: A deep-learning model trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, used to generate and summarise language (e.g. GPT, Claude, Gemini)
The data set used to teach a machine-learning model
Machine learning from labelled examples (inputs paired with correct outputs), used for classification and prediction
AI designed to perform a specific task, such as playing chess or recognising faces; all current AI is narrow (weak) AI

items.markingKey: D. "narrow AI" is AI designed to perform a specific task, such as playing chess or recognising faces; all current AI is narrow (weak) AI.

items.stem: Explain the difference between general AI and narrow AI.
items.answer: Narrow AI performs specific tasks (translation, playing Go); general AI would match human ability across any intellectual task and does not yet exist.

items.answer: Each system performs well only on the task or type of data it was designed or trained for (e.g. image recognition, text generation) and cannot transfer understanding flexibly to unrelated tasks as humans can. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Using AlphaGo v Lee Sedol (2016) as an example, explain the shift to machine learning.
items.answer: DeepMind's AlphaGo, combining deep neural networks with reinforcement learning, defeated Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul; Lee later retired, saying AI "cannot be defeated". Unlike Deep Blue, AlphaGo learned from data and self-play in a game too complex for brute force, marking a turning point in AI.

items.stem: A supervised machine-learning model is trained to identify diseased crop leaves from photos. On a test set of 184 examples it gives: true positives 30, false negatives 14, false positives 28, true negatives 112. Calculate the accuracy, the precision (TP ÷ (TP + FP)) and the recall (TP ÷ (TP + FN)). For this use, explain whether false negatives or false positives are more serious.
items.answer: accuracy 77.2%, precision 51.7%, recall 68.2%; e.g. for diseased leaves, missed cases (false negatives) usually matter more where harm from missing is high (medical, fraud), whereas false positives matter more if wrongly flagged cases are punished or annoy users
items.markingKey: Accuracy (30+112)/184 = 77.2% [A1]; precision 30/(30+28) = 51.7% [A1]; recall 30/(30+14) = 68.2% [A1]. Justified judgement on error costs in context [R1 R1].

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Turing test".
items.answer: A test proposed by Alan Turing (1950) in which a machine passes if a human judge cannot reliably tell its text conversation from a human's
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a test proposed by Alan Turing (1950) in which a machine passes if a human judge cannot reliably tell its text conversation from a human's. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "test set"?
options: A machine-learning model made of layers of connected artificial neurons whose weighted connections are adjusted during training
Data held back from training and used to evaluate how well a model performs on unseen examples
A period of reduced funding and interest in AI after expectations were not met, as in the 1970s and late 1980s
A generative model that creates images by learning to remove noise step by step, used in tools such as Stable Diffusion
items.answer: Data held back from training and used to evaluate how well a model performs on unseen examples
items.markingKey: B. "test set" is data held back from training and used to evaluate how well a model performs on unseen examples.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "deep learning"?
options: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers, which can learn complex features from large data sets
A test proposed by Alan Turing (1950) in which a machine passes if a human judge cannot reliably tell its text conversation from a human's
An AI program that uses a knowledge base of rules from human experts to make decisions, popular in the 1980s (e.g. MYCIN)
The correct answer attached to a training example, such as "spam" or "not spam"
items.answer: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers, which can learn complex features from large data sets
items.markingKey: A. "deep learning" is machine learning using neural networks with many layers, which can learn complex features from large data sets.

items.stem: Explain why all current AI systems are described as narrow AI.
items.answer: Each system performs well only on the task or type of data it was designed or trained for (e.g. image recognition, text generation) and cannot transfer understanding flexibly to unrelated tasks as humans can.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each system performs well only on the task or type of data it was designed or trained for (e.g. image recognition, text generation) and cannot transfer understanding flexibly to unrelated tasks as humans can. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the quality of training data determines the quality of a machine-learning model.
items.answer: The model can only learn patterns present in its data; if data is incomplete, unrepresentative, wrongly labelled or historically biased, the model reproduces these flaws ("garbage in, garbage out").
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The model can only learn patterns present in its data; if data is incomplete, unrepresentative, wrongly labelled or historically biased, the model reproduces these flaws ("garbage in, garbage out"). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between generative AI and discriminative (predictive) AI.
items.answer: Discriminative AI classifies or predicts from inputs (e.g. is this email spam?); generative AI creates new content resembling its training data (e.g. writing an email).
items.markingKey: Discriminative AI classifies or predicts from inputs (e.g. is this email spam?); generative AI creates new content resembling its training data (e.g. writing an email). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between narrow AI and general AI.
items.answer: Narrow AI performs specific tasks (translation, playing Go); general AI would match human ability across any intellectual task and does not yet exist.
items.markingKey: Narrow AI performs specific tasks (translation, playing Go); general AI would match human ability across any intellectual task and does not yet exist. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between test data and training data.
items.answer: Training data is used to fit the model's parameters; test data is kept separate to measure how well the model generalises to new examples.
items.markingKey: Training data is used to fit the model's parameters; test data is kept separate to measure how well the model generalises to new examples. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Generative AI copies and pastes from its training data." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Models learn statistical patterns and generate new combinations; however, they can sometimes reproduce training data closely (memorisation), which raises copyright concerns.
items.markingKey: Models learn statistical patterns and generate new combinations; however, they can sometimes reproduce training data closely (memorisation), which raises copyright concerns. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'"
— Alan Turing, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", Mind, 1950

Explain how Turing proposed to answer the question in the source.
items.answer: He replaced the question with the "imitation game": if a machine's text responses cannot be reliably distinguished from a human's by an interrogator, it can be said to behave intelligently.
items.markingKey: He replaced the question with the "imitation game": if a machine's text responses cannot be reliably distinguished from a human's by an interrogator, it can be said to behave intelligently. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A student claims: "A machine-learning model that is 99% accurate on its training data will work well in the real world." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: High training accuracy may mean overfitting; performance must be measured on unseen test data and real-world conditions, which often differ (data drift).
items.markingKey: High training accuracy may mean overfitting; performance must be measured on unseen test data and real-world conditions, which often differ (data drift). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A single artificial neuron (perceptron) decides whether a photo contains a cat. Inputs: x1 = 1, x2 = 0, x3 = 1; weights: w1 = 0.8, w2 = -0.5, w3 = 0.5. It outputs 1 if the weighted sum ≥ 0.7, otherwise 0. Calculate the weighted sum and the output.
items.answer: sum = 1.3; output 1

items.stem: A student claims: "ChatGPT is an example of artificial general intelligence." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Large language models are powerful but still narrow systems trained to predict text; they lack reliable reasoning, grounded understanding and general competence across all tasks.
items.markingKey: Large language models are powerful but still narrow systems trained to predict text; they lack reliable reasoning, grounded understanding and general competence across all tasks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A supervised machine-learning model is trained to identify diseased crop leaves from photos. On a test set of 480 examples it gives: true positives 52, false negatives 16, false positives 39, true negatives 373. Calculate the accuracy, the precision (TP ÷ (TP + FP)) and the recall (TP ÷ (TP + FN)).
items.answer: accuracy 88.5%, precision 57.1%, recall 76.5%

items.stem: A single artificial neuron (perceptron) decides whether to recommend a video. Inputs: x1 = 0, x2 = 1, x3 = 1; weights: w1 = 1.2, w2 = -0.5, w3 = -0.5. It outputs 1 if the weighted sum ≥ 1, otherwise 0. Calculate the weighted sum and the output.
items.answer: sum = -1; output 0

items.stem: Briefly describe AlphaGo v Lee Sedol (2016) and explain what it reveals about the shift to machine learning.
items.answer: DeepMind's AlphaGo, combining deep neural networks with reinforcement learning, defeated Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul; Lee later retired, saying AI "cannot be defeated". Unlike Deep Blue, AlphaGo learned from data and self-play in a game too complex for brute force, marking a turning point in AI.
items.markingKey: Context (DeepMind's AlphaGo, combining deep neural networks with reinforcement learning, defeated Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul; Lee later retired, saying AI "cannot be defeated".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: unlike Deep Blue, AlphaGo learned from data and self-play in a game too complex for brute force, marking a turning point in AI. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the shift to machine learning.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Supervised learning is more useful for society than unsupervised learning."
items.answer: Supervised learning drives many practical applications, but unsupervised and self-supervised methods are increasingly important; usefulness depends on the problem.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: powers medical diagnosis, translation, spam filtering; performance can be measured against labels. Arguments against: labelling is costly and can embed human bias; unsupervised methods find unknown patterns (fraud, genetics); many advanced systems combine both (self-supervised pre-training). Supported judgement: Supervised learning drives many practical applications, but unsupervised and self-supervised methods are increasingly important; usefulness depends on the problem.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that deep learning has made AI more powerful but less trustworthy.
items.answer: Deep learning increased capability and opacity together; trustworthiness depends on testing, transparency and oversight.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: huge gains in perception and language; opaque models (black box); hallucinations and adversarial vulnerability. Arguments against: explainability tools and evaluation are improving; older rule-based systems were brittle in other ways; trust depends on governance, not only technique. Supported judgement: Deep learning increased capability and opacity together; trustworthiness depends on testing, transparency and oversight. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "The Turing test is still a useful measure of machine intelligence." Discuss.
items.answer: It remains a useful thought experiment about behaviour, but not an adequate measure of intelligence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: simple, behavioural and influential; captures human-like communication ability. Arguments against: tests imitation, not understanding (Chinese Room); LLMs can fool people without general intelligence; ignores non-linguistic intelligence. Supported judgement: It remains a useful thought experiment about behaviour, but not an adequate measure of intelligence. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.
